description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
The project is successfully finished.
Update 14 July 2023: (inserted by MN)
The project was successfully completed, although we had to lower our ambitions in a few cases. Due to Covid-19 limitations, some things went differently than planned and the level of the intended outcomes had to be adjusted.
In the first training period, we had online lectures, self-study tasks, assignments and discussions.
The project outcomes “capacity building in sustainable aquaculture shrimp farming practices and improve contacts and communication with various stakeholders” and “Enhanced capacity in monitoring mangrove area on shrimp farms” were achieved. We **handed out 17 certificates to training participants. **
The participants described in the first training block the concepts of **efficiency and effectiveness in context of aquaculture production systems. **They also reflected on the impacts of shrimp farming practices on the environment. A local expert addressed the policy context within which shrimp farming and mangrove restoration takes place. In the second block, the participants learned the **basic principles of remote sensing** and were exposed to a method for **mangrove mapping on shrimp farms**. This was difficult in an online setting with 6 hours time difference and participants who are not always very confident in speaking English. Missing the possibility of non-verbal communication and direct, real-time interaction hampered the training and we had to lower the expectations substantially. **Not all participants managed to go through the entire mapping exercise.** However, some of them came quite far or finished. To reduce computation time we had cur out a small fragment from a high-resolution satellite image for the exercise. This means there were **no complete mangrove maps produced but mapping approaches were practiced**, demonstrated and discussed. Therefore, we managed to achieve the project outcome to “learn tools and techniques to identify the on-farm coverage of mangroves using remote sensing and GIS” but not to the level as we hoped for.
Based on the newly acquired insights in forest policies, mangrove restoration activities, shrimp farming practices and mapping and monitoring approaches we discussed with the participants how to go about “identifying, prioritizing and monitoring in the light of sustainable expansion of shrimp farming with restoration of mangroves”. So these projects outcomes were addressed in the first half and on-line part of the training. The evaluation was filled in by the majority of the participants, **16 of them, with a gender balance of 50/50. **
The second part of the training started with an online preparation for a **stakeholder workshop that we luckily could do F2F **a few weeks later. Because there was a substantial period between the training blocks, a number of participants had dropped off due to various reasons (other jobs, rescheduling the program a few times clashed with other appointments in their agendas etc.). The preparations for the stakeholder workshop with the course participants revealed adaptations that we had to make in the approach for the workshop. We found out that it would not work to give our training participants the role of moderators at the stakeholder workshop. **Most of the training participants were relative young staff members from CTU and DARD**. They **lacked the seniority** to lead discussions and provide instructions to higher-ranking people during a stakeholder workshop. The trainers, together with the local counterpart, had to take the lead.
The stakeholder workshop was extremely valuable in reaching another project output. All **participants (around 35 of different organisations** like CTU, industry, tourism, peoples committee, ministries) gained insights in how discussing each other’s’ problems in terms of cause and effect relationships boosts acceptance and support for solutions towards sustainable shrimp farming including on-farm mangroves. Due to time spent on translations and extra attention to the problem formulations we could not come to the end of the full exercise of constructing a **problem tree and converting it in an objective tree**. This part and discussing potential strategies or project ideas derived from that were addressed in a shorter demonstration and discussion session. The different workshop participants indicated that they had learned a lot from being forced to clearer problem formulation. The fact that they were obliged to specify sharper, use indicators to clarify their problems made that there were less misconceptions, and it “increased acceptance of problems perceived by other stakeholders”. This was an **important project outcome that worked even better than expected.**
The project outcomes for the **capacity building on e-learning** were achieved with a lower level than what was intended. Due to the Covid-19 pandemic the timing of the training blocks was shifted a few times and did not always fit in the agendas of the training participants. So, we had **rather low numbers of attendants (HOW MANY?). **They were exposed to different **licenced and licence-free online teaching platforms**, and **tips and tricks for designing and running on-line education**. So, we reached the project outcome however for **lower numbers of participants** (**HOW MANY?)**than we hoped for in the proposal stage. The same held for the **awareness-raising block**. Although we had a limited number of participants who could work on this, the intensive coaching of the super-enthusiastic and hardworking teams lead to very nice posters and films. The participants who were there, took their role as awareness-raisers seriously which resulted in good exposure of the training and the problems for which they produced the posters and films.

01-02-2023: Best estimated guess. Among the training participants, we had people from different Ministries, different faculties of Can Tho University, and one person from the private sector. During the stakeholder workshop, there were several guests from outside (a.o. of Ministries, the aquaculture sector, and local government) who also indicated that they benefited from training in formulating problems and from the problem tree exercise.
